quote: daher ist die Poincarésche Fragestellung nahe liegend nach solchen Bewegungen, die für $t=\infty$ sich immer mehr einem stationären oder perio- dischen Zustand nähern.
english: Hence Poincaré's way of posing the question is natural: to ask for those motions which, as $t=\infty$, approach more and more a stationary or periodic state.
topic: Notes on descending from invariant constructions to Euclidean geometry with imaginary elements, on function theory of two variables and birational transformations, on the long-term behaviour of motions in the three-body problem after Poincaré, and a plan to understand function theory from the standpoint of algebraic number theory.

triage.modern_statement: In the N-body problem (here the three-body problem), viewed as a Hamiltonian system, the question is which solutions are asymptotic as t→+∞ to an equilibrium (a stationary, e.g. central-configuration/relative-equilibrium, state) or to a periodic orbit. In modern terms, these are the solutions lying on the stable (and unstable) invariant manifolds of hyperbolic equilibria and periodic orbits. Poincaré called them 'solutions asymptotiques', and the doubly asymptotic ones are homoclinic or heteroclinic orbits. Hilbert writes this down as the natural question to ask, following Poincaré. It is a programmatic note, not a newly posed conjecture.
triage.answered_by: The question goes back to Poincaré himself, not to Hilbert. In his 1890 prize memoir and in Les Méthodes nouvelles de la mécanique céleste (1892–99), Poincaré proved that asymptotic solutions exist: families of orbits lying on two asymptotic surfaces through an unstable periodic solution of the restricted three-body problem. That work led to homoclinic tangles and chaos. The broader programme of classifying long-term ('final') motions was taken up by Chazy in 1922 and later by Sitnikov, Alekseev, Llibre–Simó and others, up to Guardia–Martín–Seara (Inventiones Math. 2016) and Capiński–Guardia–Martín–Seara–Zgliczyński. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems, nor the 24th.

evidence.claim: Poincaré (1892) took an unstable periodic solution of the circular restricted three-body problem and described a family of asymptotic solutions lying on two asymptotic surfaces.
Modern numerical work studies asymptotic, homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits around hyperbolic Lyapunov periodic orbits in restricted three-body problems.
Chazy classified the final motions of the three-body problem in 1922. Understanding its long-term dynamics is described as a longstanding question in dynamical systems.
Guardia, Martín and Seara proved that oscillatory motions exist in the restricted planar circular three-body problem for every value of the mass ratio (Inventiones Math. 203 (2016) 417–492).
Studying final motions is called one of the most important questions in the analysis of the three-body problem.

triage.why: Hilbert's note simply records Poincaré's way of posing the question, namely to look for motions that approach equilibria or periodic orbits as t→∞. Poincaré answered the existence part himself with his theory of asymptotic solutions and stable/unstable manifolds. That is why the verdict is 'solved': the specific question was answered, though by Poincaré, the person who originally asked it, and some of that work came after Hilbert's note was written. The wider long-term question (Chazy's classification of final motions, oscillatory motions, homoclinic dynamics) is still an active research area with recent results. I could not find any source tying this diary entry specifically to later work by Hilbert. Confidence is medium because the note is brief and I had to infer how it maps onto the modern question.
